entries.original_title: High in the hierarchy: How vertical location and judgments of leaders' power are interrelated
entries.original_authors: Giessner, Steffen R.; Schubert, Thomas W.
entries.original_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
entries.description: Original Study 3a claimed that describing a leader as powerful rather than powerless causes participants to place the leader's box higher in an organization chart; this was tested in the current paper's Study 1.
entries.citation_sentence: In Study 3a of the same original paper (Giessner & Schubert, 2007), we had tested the reverse effect -namely whether describing a leader as powerful versus powerless would result in placing a box of this leader on a higher versus lower vertical position within an organization chart.
entries.notes: The authors explicitly state that the preregistered Study 1 successfully replicated the main findings of the original study.

entries.original_title: High in the hierarchy: How vertical location and judgments of leaders' power are interrelated
entries.original_authors: Giessner, Steffen R.; Schubert, Thomas W.
entries.original_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
entries.description: Original Study 1a claimed that increasing the magnitude of the vertical distance between a leader and subordinates in an organization chart increases perceived power; this magnitude claim was tested in the current paper's Study 2.
entries.citation_sentence: Study 2: Following up on ManyLabs' replication failure with an adjusted paradigm of Study 1a, Giessner and Schubert (2007)
entries.notes: Study 2 found no effect of magnitude of vertical distance while rank order was held constant, and the authors describe the original positive finding as a false positive. The novel rank-order hypothesis is not coded as a separate replication entry.
